extracted.intended_audience: artisans, alchemists, glassmakers, metalworkers, apothecaries and military engineers (early-modern craftsmen)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical how‑to guidance and evaluative principles for making fine/fragile works, secret writing, distillation apparatus, glass and metalworking, and urban fortification drawn from an early‑modern technical treatise. Includes material choice, vessel and furnace design, heat regimes, and construction dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtilitas / tenuitas as an artistic and technical virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The work's 'subtility' (extreme thinness, fineness, minuteness) is a mark of skill and artifice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True subtility is valuable when joined to utility; mere fragile or ornamental minuteness that is not durable or useful is vain. Very thin/fragile works may produce admiration but often lack durability or practical value. The author distinguishes examples that are useful from those that are mere toys or luxuries and warns that some subtilities are ephemeral and soon perish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of material for large mechanical spheres / celestial machines (glass vs metal)
rubrics_metrics.description: When constructing machines that imitate celestial spheres, material choice determines transparency, durability, and feasible size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Glass gives transparency (permitting inner inspection) but is fragile and cannot be made very large without breaking; metal (iron/bronze) is stronger and preferable for durable, large machines. For very delicate transparent parts glass may be used, but metal is necessary for long‑lived, heavy, or moving structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of geared/denticulated wheels and transmitted motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Design of wheels with teeth (denticulis) and compound wheels arranged to transmit and transform motion without external ropes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple toothed wheels in axles so one wheel engages another, allowing self‑contained motion. Examples include arrangements to make chairs, seats, or thrones move while appearing immobile; use of three iron circles with mobile poles for compound motion. Ensure interleaving of teeth and correct placement of axes to achieve continuous rotation and desired mechanical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secret (occult) writing — three principal methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Three distinct methods for hiding written content: encoded letters, transposition/rolled‑membrane (scytale‑like) devices, and invisible/latent inks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Letter‑substitution/cipher: compress or alter letter sequences so the obvious sentence is unrecognizable; supply an exemplar key to the recipient. 2) Membrane/transposition: write sentences across multiple thin membranes with aligned holes or punched patterns so that when stacked/rolled the message appears to those with the template. 3) Invisible inks: write with substances that are invisible in water but appear by heat or chemical exposure (e.g., onion juice, certain plant juices), or write with materials that appear when exposed to fire; such methods require careful preparation and handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materials for writing and books (papyrus, parchment, wax, metal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of writing substrate affects durability, readability, and suitability for secret or permanent texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Egyptian papyrus was excellent for certain uses but not always durable; parchment (membrane from skins) is the most durable of ordinary papers and valued for longevity. Wax and lead were used for temporary or special purposes (e.g., inscriptions); make choices based on whether permanence, thinness, whiteness, or ease of handling is desired. Printing technologies later changed optimal choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of distillation (one‑vessel, two‑vessel, three‑vessel / 'Bozia'/'conceptaculum')
rubrics_metrics.description: Distillation can be carried out in several configurations: single vessel (where volatile parts condense within same vessel), two vessels (either circulating back or directing to a second vessel), or three vessels (a specialized setup with a 'pileus' or cap and intermediate chamber).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One‑vessel distillation is for materials that spontaneously burn/volatilize; two‑vessel methods permit either circulation (returns condensate to same vessel) or collection in another vessel; three‑vessel systems (called 'Bozia' by barbarians or the 'conceptaculum' with a pileus) have a cap with multiple holes and a receiving vessel—these are used when more controlled separation is needed. Choose configuration by material volatility and desired purity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material choice for distilling vessels (metal, earthenware, glass, lead, silver, gold)
rubrics_metrics.description: The composition of distilling vessels strongly influences purity, durability, and behavior under heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earthenware (figulina) is generally recommended for many distillations; iron, copper, and lead are common but may taint the product. Glass is excellent for pure distillates if it is white, well‑fired, and properly annealed; it must be free of flaws and slowly cooled to avoid breakage. Use lead for some constructions but be aware of odor/taste issues. For certain operations silver and gold have roles but are costly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat application methods in distillation (direct, quantity, interposed layers, water bath)
rubrics_metrics.description: How heat is applied—its source, continuity, intensity and whether it is interposed—determines distillation behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heat may be from the substance itself (sun), by the amount/strength of fire, by interposing substances (ashes, earth, water) to moderate heat, or by using a water bath (balneum) for gentle, uniform heating. Gentle, prolonged low heat is needed for delicate separations; sudden intense heat causes loss of volatile virtues. Choose method to avoid decomposition while achieving separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design features of furnaces and retorts (foramina, spiracula, pileus, multiple mouths)
rubrics_metrics.description: Furnace and vessel geometry—perforated bottoms, vents for fire, upper openings for tempering, and multiple mouths—influence ease of feeding fire, control of heat, and smoke extraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In multi‑vessel furnaces ensure the base is perforated to admit airflow; provide lower vents (spiracula) for feeding the fire and upper holes to temper or moderate heat. A 'pileus' (cap) should be sized to collect vapors and permit condensation; multiple mouths allow even heating. For very acrid vapors use long vessels and capacious pilei to avoid breakage and to collect vapors effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of circulation and reciprocal heating to manage distillation
rubrics_metrics.description: Returning condensate (circulation) or mutual reciprocal heating slows the net heating and allows better separation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reciprocal/circulatory setups reduce heat intensity on the material and preserve volatile virtues longer. Repeated mild circulations may require long time (many hours/days) but preserve delicate properties; in contrast, straightforward direct distillation with strong fire is faster but wastes virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fractionation and yield expectations in repeated distillations
rubrics_metrics.description: Yields decline with successive distillations; different fractions contain differing amounts of the desired virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically about half the volatile substance is obtained in the first distillation, less in the second, and scant amounts by the third or fourth—after which returns are negligible. Consider diminishing returns when deciding the number of distillations and when to stop to preserve resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventing metal liquefaction failure: crusts, embedded stones, and humidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Three main causes prevent metal from liquefying: cold crusts on the surface, materials adherent at the vessel bottom, and water/moisture in the matrix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break or remove hard crusts that cool and insulate the metal; ensure vessels are not filled with materials that hold humidity (such as certain stones) which vaporize and impede melting; avoid having molten metal lie directly on a deep bottom (which chills it). Use dry, heat‑retaining supports and appropriate fluxes or heating techniques to overcome these problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitating metal melting and fusion (choice of fluxes and co‑materials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain stones, fluxes and coals assist the liquefaction of metals by altering heat transmission and chemical environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additives such as sal nitrum, alum, or suitable lapides can help when distilling 'acrid' waters or dissolving ores; choose coals and woods that maintain the proper type of fire (long steady vs intense). Use materials familiar to the process: marble, galena, or other minerals can aid liquefaction, but beware that some humid stones impede melting until thoroughly dried.

rubrics_metrics.name: Softening and shaping horn (horn working method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Method to make horn malleable for shaping into vessels or tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soak horn in a mixture (e.g., water with ashes), heat until pliable, insert a rounded iron rod or core, hammer and shape while warm, then cool in water to harden. Repeat heating and hammering as needed until the piece reaches desired shape and solidity. Provide supporting boards with holes to fix the horn while working.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glass production and annealing to avoid breakage
rubrics_metrics.description: Glass intended for vessels/ampullae must be made and cooled properly to avoid fragility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use white (clear) glass that has been long cooked in the furnace and thoroughly purified. Glass must be slowly cooled and subjected to gradual tempering (avoid abrupt exposure to intense heat/cold) to prevent cracking. When intended for distillation/ampullae, ensure glass is evenly thin but not brittle; craftsmen must be skilled and ovens properly managed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charcoal / fuel preparation and placement for intense heating
rubrics_metrics.description: Type of wood/charcoal and its placement (e.g., in parabolic iron containers) affect intensity and focus of heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charcoal made from valley trees (richer, denser) often yields better heat than rarer mountain wood. Place the material in parabolic iron vessels centered on the furnace to concentrate heat; ensure iron used is polished/treated and that coals are made and stored to provide desired, steady heat for metallurgical reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of fortification — triplex defense (aqua, fossa, muro) and wall design
rubrics_metrics.description: A city's defense should be organized in three arts: water (moat), ditch, and wall—each making approach difficult and the whole near‑impregnable if properly dimensioned and constructed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make triple works—moat, ditch, and wall—so attackers cannot easily approach by ascent; use steep inclines and multiple successive earthworks to impede assault. Walls must be thick, with external round parts (battlements/towers), foundations projecting and cavities for passage, internal galleries and drains (cloacae) for sanitation and defense. Include secret passages, hidden chambers, and nearby wooded areas to conceal supplies and launch sorties. Use measured dimensions (heights and thickness in passus) appropriate to the town's size and situation.
